coverage.assessment: The 'women and children first' logic and the oilskin packet survive. The three-day instruction now omits the man's 'down and out' gloss and 'personal column'; this is a defensible compression with some cost.
The time, ship, girl and man are clear, and the hand-off is intact. The cut stage direction 'He lowered his voice' leaves the loud goodbye without its contrast. 'Made her start and turn' is also cut.
Paragraph 9 now runs two adjacent quotations with no beat between them. Her reply in paragraph 12 no longer answers 'Have you the nerve to go through with it?'
'I don't think I have, but one never knows' and 'may make all the difference' are kept. The loss of 'than with me' is negligible.
Nothing is disclosed early, and the man stays unnamed. The man's mystery, which the source filters through her imagination, is now stated flatly by the narrator; this is minor.
The grave, short exchanges are kept. 'I guess' and 'real proud' preserve her American idiom. The remaining rhythm losses are covered under the dialogue findings.
The contrast between the steadfast girl and the fearful man, and her patriotic acceptance, both survive.
Dependencies 0 and 1 are intact at both ends. For dependency 2, the local warning survives, but the 026 partner drops 'didn't think so', so the echo is weaker.

strengths: All four verbatim passages (V1–V4) survive exactly, including the quiet climactic oilskin sentence set as its own paragraph.
The girl's American idiom ('I guess you've no right', 'real proud to be chosen') and her grave, steadfast portrait are kept.
The man's paradox, overmastering fear yet unafraid of death, is preserved with the source's exclamation intact.
summary: The revision keeps every planned essential, all four verbatim excerpts, and the girl's and man's anonymity. Its own cuts cause small dialogue and staging losses. Removing 'He lowered his voice' leaves two back-to-back quotations and removes the hushed/loud contrast that explains the cover goodbye. Cutting 'I'll go through with it all right' leaves the man's 'nerve' question unanswered. The first draft had already dropped 'you'll know I'm down and out'; the revision also cuts 'personal column'. Together these thin the advertisement mechanism. None of these breaks the plot.
